name: The 1960s
line: Question what you were handed, show up in person, and make something with your own hands.

quote.text: We are as gods and might as well get good at it.
quote.source: The first line of the statement of purpose in the Whole Earth Catalog, autumn 1968

quotes.text: And so, my fellow Americans: ask not what your country can do for you, ask what you can do for your country.
I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character.
quotes.source: Speech at the Lincoln Memorial, March on Washington, 28 August 1963

quotes.text: I’m sick and tired of being sick and tired.
quotes.source: Speech with Malcolm X at Williams Institutional CME Church, Harlem, 20 December 1964

quotes.text: We are people of this generation, bred in at least modest comfort, housed now in universities, looking uncomfortably to the world we inherit.
quotes.source: The opening sentence of the Port Huron Statement, June 1962, drafted by Tom Hayden

quotes.text: There’s a time when the operation of the machine becomes so odious, makes you so sick at heart, that you can’t take part.
quotes.source: Speech on the steps of Sproul Hall, Berkeley, 2 December 1964

quotes.text: That’s one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
quotes.source: On stepping onto the Moon, 20 July 1969. He said he meant to say a man

words.meaning: The civil rights struggle, and later all the causes together
words.usage: People spoke of being in the Movement as one might speak of a calling. By 1968 the word covered peace, students, women and more.

words.meaning: Occupying a place and refusing to leave
words.usage: Four students sat at a whites-only lunch counter in Greensboro on 1 February 1960. Within two months the tactic had spread to more than fifty cities.

words.meaning: An all-night open seminar on a public question
words.usage: Invented at the University of Michigan in March 1965 by faculty who wanted to protest the war without striking.

words.meaning: A gathering with no purpose but to be together
words.usage: The Human Be-In filled a field in Golden Gate Park in January 1967 with poets, bands and some twenty thousand people.

words.meaning: One who rode interstate buses to test desegregation
words.usage: Black and white volunteers rode together into the South in 1961 and were beaten and jailed for it.

words.meaning: Resistance without injury to the opponent
words.usage: A discipline learned from Gandhi and taught in church basements, where volunteers practised being struck without striking back.

words.meaning: A society reconciled, with no one left out
words.usage: King’s name for the goal of the struggle. The aim was friendship with the opponent, not victory over him.

words.meaning: A hymn or spiritual reworded for the struggle
words.usage: Sung in mass meetings, on marches and in jail cells to give courage and to keep a crowd together.

words.meaning: People sharing in the decisions that shape their lives
words.usage: The central idea of the Port Huron Statement of 1962.

words.meaning: The student radicalism of the decade
words.usage: New because it turned from the party discipline of the old left toward moral protest and direct action.

words.meaning: Those who hold power and set the rules
words.usage: Borrowed from Britain. Government, business, the universities and the press seen as one settled interest.

words.meaning: A way of life set against the mainstream
words.usage: The historian Theodore Roszak made the word common in 1969 to describe the young who rejected a technocratic society.

words.meaning: A member of the counterculture
words.usage: A newspaper word from 1965, at first a put-down. It comes from hip, meaning in the know.

words.meaning: Conventional; not in the know
words.usage: Jazz slang from the 1940s that the young of the sixties took over.

words.meaning: Excellent
words.usage: From the groove of a record. To be in the groove was to play well.

words.meaning: Remarkable; beyond the ordinary
words.usage: Jazz talk for adventurous playing before it became all-purpose praise.

words.meaning: To understand and appreciate
words.usage: From African American speech. To dig something was to get it all the way down.

words.meaning: To talk openly and at length
words.usage: A rap session was a frank group conversation. The word came from African American English.

words.meaning: The feeling a person or place gives off
words.usage: Short for vibrations.

words.meaning: An art event in which the audience takes part
words.usage: Allan Kaprow coined it in 1959 for performances with no stage and no fixed ending.

words.meaning: A household that shares property and work
words.usage: Several thousand were founded in the United States in the second half of the decade, most of them short-lived.

words.meaning: Small independent newspapers of the counterculture
words.usage: Cheap offset printing made them possible. By 1969 there were several hundred, sharing stories through a common syndicate.

words.meaning: Small groups of women speaking from experience
words.usage: Begun in New York in 1967. Going round the circle showed that private troubles had common causes.

words.meaning: Private life is shaped by public power
words.usage: The title given to an essay by Carol Hanisch written in 1969. It became the motto of the women’s movement.

words.meaning: Self-determination and pride for Black Americans
words.usage: Stokely Carmichael raised the cry on a march in Mississippi in June 1966.

words.meaning: Black American feeling, style and music
words.usage: Gospel fervour carried into secular song, and a word of recognition between people.

words.meaning: The gulf between the young and their parents
words.usage: Nearly half of all Americans were under twenty-five in the middle of the decade.

words.meaning: Disarming force with gentleness
words.usage: The poet Allen Ginsberg proposed in 1965 that marchers hand flowers to police and soldiers.

words.meaning: The oral contraceptive
words.usage: Approved in the United States on 9 May 1960. Within five years six and a half million American women were taking it.

words.meaning: The planet as one closed vessel with a single crew
words.usage: A phrase used by Adlai Stevenson in 1965 and by Buckminster Fuller. The first photographs from the Moon made it visible.

practices.name: Hold a teach-in
practices.instructions: Pick one public question that troubles you and that you only half understand. Spend thirty minutes learning it properly. Read one primary source, not a summary: the law itself, the report, the speech, the figures. Then write three sentences of what you now know and what you still do not. The rule of this Onda is to know the facts first.
practices.why: Teach-ins began at the University of Michigan in 1965 as all-night sessions of lectures and debate. They were a way of replacing slogans with knowledge.
variations: Read the actual text of a law.
Look at the numbers behind a claim.
Explain what you learned to a friend.

practices.name: Use your own hands
practices.instructions: Make, mend or grow one thing today in place of buying it. Bake the bread, patch the jeans, fix the tap, build the shelf, plant the seeds, print the leaflet. Find the tool and the instructions first, then do it yourself from start to finish. The rule of this Onda is to make it yourself.
practices.why: The Whole Earth Catalog of 1968 gave readers access to tools and ideas for doing things themselves. Its motto was access to tools.
variations: Mend something instead of replacing it.

practices.name: Granola for breakfast
practices.instructions: Bake a tray of granola: mix rolled oats, nuts, seeds and a handful of coconut with honey and oil, and bake it low and slow, stirring now and then until golden. Eat it with yoghurt and fruit. Granola became a symbol of the natural-foods movement in the 1960s. Make a jar to share.
practices.why: Granola was reinvented in the sixties as wholesome food for people who wanted to eat close to the source. Home-baked, it is better than anything bought.
variations: Give a jar to a neighbour.

practices.name: Sing one freedom song
practices.instructions: Sing one verse of a freedom song while you get ready: We Shall Overcome, This Little Light of Mine, Keep Your Eyes on the Prize or Swing Low. Learn the words from a recording first. Singing together carried the Civil Rights Movement through jails, marches and mass meetings. Sing it with a full voice.
practices.why: Freedom songs were the heart of the movement, adapted from spirituals and hymns. A single verse in the morning is a firm start.

practices.name: A postcard to an official
practices.instructions: Write a short postcard or letter to an elected official about one issue you care about. State the issue in a line, say what you want, and sign your name and address. Be polite and specific. Post it today. Letters from voters were a tool of the movement as much as marches.
practices.why: Writing to officials was an everyday part of the movement’s work. A short, clear letter from a constituent has real weight.
variations: Write a thank-you to an official who did well.
Ask a friend to write too.

practices.name: Spaceship Earth
practices.instructions: Look at the Earthrise photograph from Apollo 8, taken on Christmas Eve 1968, and then choose one thing you waste and cut it for a day: water, electricity, food, plastic. Buckminster Fuller called the planet Spaceship Earth, a ship with limited supplies. Make a note of what you saved.
practices.why: The Earthrise photograph, showing the planet as a small blue marble, helped launch the environmental movement. It still reminds us that we share one ship.
variations: Skip a single-use item all day.
Turn off lights as you leave.

practices.name: Put your body there
practices.instructions: Choose one thing you believe is wrong and do something about it in person today, peacefully. Go to the meeting. Stand in the vigil. Carry the petition door to door. Volunteer for the shift. Write to the official and sign it. Do it with your own body in the room, not just on a screen. The rule of this Onda is to show up in person.
practices.why: The movement’s power came from people showing up: sit-ins, marches and boycotts. A physical presence says more than a comment online.

practices.name: Sit at the lunch counter
practices.instructions: Eat lunch today with someone you do not usually sit with: a person from another team, another age, another background. Ask a real question and listen. On 1 February 1960, four students sat down at a whites-only lunch counter in Greensboro and refused to leave. Their courage began a wave. Sit down with someone new, and make them welcome. The rule is to leave no one out.
practices.why: The Greensboro sit-ins spread to dozens of cities within weeks and brought down segregation in many places. A lunch with someone new is a modest echo.
variations: Sit at a different table at work.
Ask what they would like you to know.

practices.name: Throw a Frisbee
practices.instructions: Go to a park with a friend and throw a Frisbee back and forth for twenty minutes. The flying disc was invented in 1957 and became a craze on sixties campuses. Learn a backhand throw and try to catch with one hand. Laugh at the misses. Wear sunscreen if it is sunny.
practices.why: The Frisbee captured the easy optimism of the sixties: a cheap toy, a lawn and a friend. It is still a joy.

practices.name: Open a free store
practices.instructions: Set up a free store: put a box of things you no longer need on a table by your door or at work with a sign saying take what you need, leave what you can. The Diggers of San Francisco opened a free store in 1966 on the principle that goods should be shared. Offer clothes, books and tools. Return the next day to see what changed.
practices.why: The Diggers’ free store gave away goods for nothing. A small box on a table recreates the idea.
variations: Put out a box of books.

practices.name: A game of Twister
practices.instructions: Play Twister with friends or family, the party game of 1966 in which the human body is the board. Spin the spinner, put a hand or foot on the coloured circle and try not to fall. Roll out the mat, laugh and make a human pretzel. Mind your joints and play on a soft floor.
practices.why: Twister was a sensation in 1966 and a symbol of the playful, physical spirit of the decade. It is a perfect party game.
variations: Make a mat from chalk outside.

practices.name: Listen to someone’s experience
practices.instructions: Ask a friend or family member to tell you about an experience of unfair treatment, a hard time or a struggle, and listen without interrupting or offering advice. Consciousness-raising groups in the 1960s began with women telling their stories in circles, and found that private troubles were shared ones. Thank them for trusting you.
practices.why: Consciousness-raising grew from the conviction that personal experience is political. Listening to a story is the first step.
variations: Listen to an older person’s story.
Share a story of your own afterwards.

practices.name: Go round the circle
practices.instructions: Sit down with two or more people and choose one question about your own lives, such as what you were taught to want. Go round in turn. Each person speaks from their own experience for a few minutes while the others listen without interrupting or advising. At the end, say what you heard in common. Leave no one out.
practices.why: The talking circle, a practice of the women’s and civil rights movements, treats every voice as equal. It is how decisions were made in participatory democracy.
variations: Limit each speaker to three minutes.
End with one thing each person will do.

practices.name: Play the whole record
practices.instructions: Choose one album and listen to it from the first track to the last, in order, doing nothing else. No phone and no skipping. Sit or lie where you can hear it well, with others if you can. Read the sleeve. If it is a record, turn it over at the halfway point. Try Pet Sounds, A Love Supreme or Aretha’s first Atlantic album.
practices.why: The long-playing album became an art form in the sixties. Listening from start to finish is how it was meant to be heard.

practices.name: Sing along
practices.instructions: Play a folk record and sing along: Dylan, Joan Baez, Pete Seeger, Peter, Paul and Mary. Choose a song with a chorus and sing out. If you play guitar, strum it. Folk songs of the 1960s were shared in coffee houses and at rallies. Sing with others if you can.
practices.why: The folk revival was the soundtrack of the early sixties, with songs of protest and hope. Singing along puts you inside the music.
variations: Learn the chords of one song.
Write a verse of your own.

practices.name: Make a poster
practices.instructions: Design and make a poster for a cause you care about, in the bold, hand-lettered style of the Fillmore posters or the civil rights placards. Choose a short message and a strong image. Use paint, markers or cut paper. Hang it in your window or carry it to a meeting. The silkscreen and the printing press were tools of the movements.
practices.why: Wes Wilson, Victor Moscoso and others created a new poster art for the San Francisco ballrooms. Poster-making was also central to every march.
variations: Make a poster for a local event.

practices.name: Look at the Earth
practices.instructions: Go outside after dark and look at the moon, and think of the Apollo astronauts who looked back at the Earth from there. In July 1969, 600 million people watched the landing on television. Hold a thought of the whole planet, and of everyone on it. Then go in.
practices.why: The space programme of the sixties gave humanity its first view of Earth as a whole. Looking at the moon remembers it.
variations: Find the Sea of Tranquility on the moon.
Read the plaque left on the moon.

practices.name: A letter from a cell
practices.instructions: Read part of Martin Luther King Jr.’s 1963 letter, written from a cell in Birmingham, Alabama, to clergymen who had called his campaign untimely. Read the passage beginning with the line that injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere. Read aloud if you can. Think about who is waiting too long today.
practices.why: The letter is among the great pieces of American prose and a plain statement of why nonviolent direct action is needed. It repays reading aloud.
variations: Underline the line that moves you.

practices.name: A teach-in with friends
practices.instructions: Hold a teach-in on a topic in your area: invite a few friends and perhaps a speaker, read a short text together and discuss it for two hours. End with a list of three things each person will do. Share a pot of soup and bread. The rule is to know the facts first and to leave no one out.
practices.why: Teach-ins were all-night sessions of learning and debate at campuses across America in 1965. A small one at home carries on the idea.

practices.name: A day of service
practices.instructions: Spend two hours volunteering on a cause: a community garden, a food bank, a cleanup, a tutoring programme. Turn up on time, do the work asked of you and thank the organisers. Freedom Summer in 1964 brought hundreds of volunteers to Mississippi to register voters and teach. Offer your body and your time.
practices.why: The ethic of service and solidarity runs through the 1960s movements. A morning of real work is a good response.
variations: Choose an organisation you have not tried.

immersePlan.name: Read Letter from Birmingham Jail
immersePlan.text: Read King’s 1963 letter in full. It takes about thirty minutes. Underline the sentence that most challenges you.

immersePlan.name: Read from Silent Spring
immersePlan.text: Read the opening fable and a chapter of Rachel Carson’s 1962 book, which launched the environmental movement. Note how she writes.

immersePlan.name: Read The Fire Next Time
immersePlan.text: Read the opening letter to his nephew in James Baldwin’s 1963 essay. Read it aloud.

immersePlan.name: Watch an episode of Eyes on the Prize
immersePlan.text: Watch the first episode of Henry Hampton’s documentary on the civil rights movement, about Emmett Till and the Montgomery bus boycott.

immersePlan.name: Watch Summer of Soul
immersePlan.text: Watch Questlove’s 2021 documentary of the Harlem Cultural Festival of 1969, with Stevie Wonder, Nina Simone and Sly Stone. It is joyful.

immersePlan.name: Watch Woodstock
immersePlan.text: Watch part of Michael Wadleigh’s 1970 documentary of the festival. Notice the crowd and the mud.

immersePlan.name: Listen to A Love Supreme
immersePlan.text: Play John Coltrane’s 1965 suite in four parts, a prayer in sound. Listen from start to finish in the dark.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Pet Sounds
immersePlan.text: Play the Beach Boys’ 1966 album of lush harmonies and yearning. Hear it all the way through.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Aretha Franklin
immersePlan.text: Play Aretha Franklin’s 1967 album, with Respect and Do Right Woman. Sing along and dance.

immersePlan.name: Look at Earthrise
immersePlan.text: Look at William Anders’s photograph of the Earth rising over the moon, taken from Apollo 8. Look for a full minute.

immersePlan.name: Look at The Problem We All Live With
immersePlan.text: Look at Norman Rockwell’s 1964 painting of six-year-old Ruby Bridges walking to school guarded by federal marshals. Look at the wall.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Fillmore posters
immersePlan.text: Look at the swirling psychedelic posters of the San Francisco ballrooms. Pick one and try to read its lettering.

immersePlan.name: Make granola
immersePlan.text: Bake rolled oats with nuts, seeds and honey until golden. Eat it with yoghurt.

immersePlan.name: Cook beans and cornbread
immersePlan.text: Cook a big pot of beans and a pan of cornbread, as movement kitchens did for a crowd. Share it.

immersePlan.name: Share a fondue
immersePlan.text: Dip bread and vegetables into a common pot of melted cheese or chocolate, the party food of the sixties. Eat with friends.

immersePlan.name: Drink coffee at a counter
immersePlan.text: Sit at a counter with a cup of filter coffee. Think of those who sat at the counters in 1960 and what it cost them.

immersePlan.name: Brew a pot of herbal tea
immersePlan.text: Brew peppermint or chamomile and share a pot with a friend. Sip slowly.

immersePlan.name: Mix a glass of Tang
immersePlan.text: Mix a glass of the powdered orange drink that went to space with John Glenn in 1962. Or mix any orange squash and drink it as an astronaut.

immersePlan.name: Sing together
immersePlan.text: Sing a freedom song or folk song with others. Even two people count.

immersePlan.name: Give something away
immersePlan.text: Put out one thing you no longer need with a sign saying free, and see who takes it.

immersePlan.name: Write a pledge of nonviolence
immersePlan.text: Write a short commitment to deal with anger and conflict without violence, as civil rights volunteers signed. Sign it and keep it.

immersePlan.name: Throw a Frisbee
immersePlan.text: Throw a flying disc with a friend in the park. Learn a backhand throw.

immersePlan.name: Play Twister
immersePlan.text: Play the party game of 1966 with friends or family. Spin, stretch and try not to fall.

immersePlan.name: Play circle games
immersePlan.text: Keep a small footbag in the air with a circle of friends, using only feet and knees. Count passes.

immersePlan.name: Mark Martin Luther King Jr. Day
immersePlan.text: On the third Monday of January, read a speech of King’s and do an act of service. Listen to I Have a Dream.

immersePlan.name: Mark Earth Day
immersePlan.text: On 22 April, spend an hour outdoors and plant something or clean a stretch of ground.

immersePlan.name: Mark Juneteenth
immersePlan.text: On 19 June, read about the end of slavery in Texas in 1865, and support a Black-owned business or cause.

immersePlan.name: Practise teach-in
immersePlan.text: A teach-in is a gathering to learn about an issue. Spend half an hour learning about one issue today.

immersePlan.name: Practise beloved community
immersePlan.text: The beloved community is King’s vision of a society based on justice and love. Do one thing today to include someone.

immersePlan.name: Practise consciousness-raising
immersePlan.text: Consciousness-raising is sharing experience to see what is common. Listen to someone’s story today.

rules.why: Custom is not an argument. Ask who benefits and whether it is true.
Read the source before you raise your voice. A protest is only as good as its case.
A cause needs bodies in the room, not opinions held at a distance.
Refuse to hate the people you oppose. The means decide what the end will be.
Cook, mend, build and play your own music. Do not only consume.
Freedom for some is not freedom. Ask who is missing from the room.

read.title: Letter from Birmingham Jail
read.creator: Martin Luther King Jr.
read.why: Written in the margins of a newspaper in a cell, to white clergymen who had asked him to wait. The clearest defence of civil disobedience in English.

read.title: Silent Spring
read.creator: Rachel Carson
read.why: A marine biologist shows what pesticides were doing to birds, rivers and people. The modern environmental movement begins here.

read.title: The Fire Next Time
read.creator: James Baldwin
read.why: Two essays on race and faith in America, one of them a letter to his nephew. Short and unsparing.

read.title: The Feminine Mystique
read.creator: Betty Friedan
read.why: On the unhappiness of educated women confined to the home, which she called the problem that has no name.

read.title: Slouching Towards Bethlehem
read.creator: Joan Didion
read.why: Essays from California, including a cool and troubled report from Haight-Ashbury in 1967.

read.title: The Autobiography of Malcolm X
read.creator: Malcolm X with Alex Haley
read.why: From street hustler to prison convert to minister to pilgrim. A life that changed direction more than once.

watch.title: Eyes on the Prize
watch.creator: Henry Hampton, executive producer
watch.why: Fourteen hours on the civil rights movement told by those who were in it. The standard documentary history.

watch.title: Summer of Soul
watch.creator: Ahmir Thompson, known as Questlove
watch.why: Footage of the 1969 Harlem Cultural Festival, unseen for fifty years, with Nina Simone, Stevie Wonder and Sly Stone.

watch.title: Woodstock
watch.creator: Michael Wadleigh
watch.why: Three hours from three days in a field in August 1969, as much about the crowd as the bands.

watch.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey
watch.creator: Stanley Kubrick
watch.why: From the first tool to a voyage beyond Jupiter. The film that showed what cinema could attempt.

listen.title: A Love Supreme
listen.creator: John Coltrane
listen.why: A four-part suite of thanksgiving recorded in one evening by his quartet.

listen.title: Pet Sounds
listen.creator: The Beach Boys
listen.why: Brian Wilson’s studio symphony of longing, built from harpsichords, bicycle bells and stacked voices.

listen.title: I Never Loved a Man the Way I Love You
listen.creator: Aretha Franklin
listen.why: The record that made her the Queen of Soul. It opens with her version of Respect.

listen.title: Are You Experienced
listen.creator: The Jimi Hendrix Experience
listen.why: The electric guitar turned into something no one had heard before.

listen.title: The Freewheelin’ Bob Dylan
listen.creator: Bob Dylan
listen.why: A twenty-one-year-old with a guitar and a harmonica writes the songs the decade would march to.

art.title: Earthrise
art.creator: William Anders, Apollo 8
art.why: The Earth, blue and half in shadow, rising over the grey horizon of the Moon. The first time people saw their planet from elsewhere in colour.

art.title: Campbell’s Soup Cans
art.creator: Andy Warhol
art.why: Thirty-two canvases, one for each flavour, hung in a row like goods on a shelf. In the Museum of Modern Art, New York.

art.title: The Problem We All Live With
art.creator: Norman Rockwell
art.why: Six-year-old Ruby Bridges walks to school between federal marshals, past a wall marked with a slur and a thrown tomato.

art.title: The Fillmore posters
art.creator: Wes Wilson, Victor Moscoso and others
art.why: Concert bills from San Francisco in vibrating colours and lettering that melts, meant to be puzzled out slowly.

eat.title: Granola
eat.creator: Rolled oats baked with honey and nuts
eat.why: A nineteenth-century health food that the counterculture revived and made its emblem.

eat.title: Brown rice and vegetables
eat.creator: A whole-grain bowl
eat.why: The staple of the natural food cooperatives and macrobiotic kitchens that opened in the second half of the decade.

eat.title: A pot of beans and cornbread
eat.creator: Cooked for a crowd
eat.why: Cheap, filling and shared. The food of movement kitchens, church suppers and communes.

eat.title: Fondue
eat.creator: Bread dipped in a common pot of melted cheese
eat.why: The dinner party fashion of the suburban sixties, eaten from one pot in the middle of the table.

drink.title: Coffee at a lunch counter
drink.creator: Filter coffee in a thick cup
drink.why: What the four students in Greensboro asked for and were refused.

drink.title: Herbal tea
drink.creator: Peppermint or chamomile
drink.why: The counterculture’s alternative to coffee, sold loose in the new health food stores.

drink.title: Tang
drink.creator: A powdered orange drink
drink.why: Flown on John Glenn’s orbital flight in 1962 and marketed ever after as the drink of the astronauts.

customs.title: Singing together
customs.creator: Freedom songs and folk songs
customs.why: A meeting began and ended with a song, arms crossed and hands joined, everyone swaying.

customs.title: The free store
customs.creator: Goods given away
customs.why: The Diggers of San Francisco ran shops where everything was free and served a free meal in the park each afternoon.

customs.title: The pledge of nonviolence
customs.creator: A signed commitment
customs.why: Volunteers in Birmingham in 1963 signed ten commandments, among them to refrain from violence of fist, tongue or heart.

customs.title: The two-finger sign
customs.creator: A greeting of peace
customs.why: Churchill’s wartime V for victory, turned by the young into a wish for peace.

games.title: Frisbee
games.creator: Flying disc · United States
games.why: A plastic disc thrown for the pleasure of it. Students in New Jersey invented a team game with it in 1968.

games.title: Twister
games.creator: Party game · United States
games.why: Players stretch across a mat of coloured circles. It sold three million copies in its first year after being played on television.

games.title: Spacewar
games.creator: Computer game · United States
games.why: Two ships duel around a star. Written by students at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, it was one of the first video games.

games.title: Hacky sack and circle games
games.creator: Cooperative play · United States
games.why: Games with no winner, in which the aim is only to keep the thing going.

festivals.title: Martin Luther King Jr. Day
festivals.creator: The third Monday of January
festivals.why: A national holiday in the United States since 1986, kept as a day of service.

festivals.title: Earth Day
festivals.creator: 22 April
festivals.why: First held in 1970, when twenty million Americans took part. It grew directly from the sixties.

festivals.title: Juneteenth
festivals.creator: 19 June
festivals.why: Marks the end of slavery in Texas in 1865. Civil rights marchers carried it across the country in 1968.

festivals.title: Newport Folk Festival
festivals.creator: Late July, Newport, Rhode Island
festivals.why: Where the folk revival gathered, and where Dylan played an electric guitar in 1965 to cheers and boos.

places.title: International Civil Rights Center and Museum
places.creator: Greensboro, North Carolina
places.why: The former Woolworth store. The lunch counter and its stools are still in place where the four students sat.

places.title: Edmund Pettus Bridge
places.creator: Selma, Alabama
places.why: Where state troopers attacked six hundred marchers on 7 March 1965. Two weeks later twenty-five thousand walked from here to Montgomery.

places.title: The Lincoln Memorial
places.creator: Washington, D.C.
places.why: An inscription on the steps marks where King stood before a quarter of a million people in August 1963.

places.title: Haight-Ashbury
places.creator: San Francisco, California
places.why: The few blocks of Victorian houses beside Golden Gate Park that became the centre of the counterculture in 1967.

places.title: Bethel Woods
places.creator: Bethel, New York
places.why: The sloping dairy field where the Woodstock festival was held, now a museum and concert ground.

places.title: Kennedy Space Center
places.creator: Cape Canaveral, Florida
places.why: The launch pads of the Moon flights, with a Saturn V rocket lying on its side under one roof.

ethics.title: Nonviolence
ethics.text: Resist the wrong without hating or harming the person who does it.
ethics.practice: Speak to an opponent today as someone you hope to win over.

ethics.title: Dissent
ethics.text: Loyalty sometimes takes the form of refusal.
ethics.practice: Say no, politely and openly, to one thing you think is wrong.

ethics.title: Equality
ethics.text: No one is to be kept out because of who they are.
ethics.practice: Notice who is absent from a room you are in, and ask why.

ethics.title: Authenticity
ethics.text: Live by what you actually believe, not by appearances.
ethics.practice: Drop one thing you do only for show.

ethics.title: Community
ethics.text: Share housing, food, tools and work.
ethics.practice: Lend something, or share a meal with people you do not usually eat with.

ethics.title: Care for the Earth
ethics.text: The planet is finite and everything in it is connected.
ethics.practice: Find out where one thing you threw away today will end up.

philosophy.title: Civil disobedience
philosophy.text: King argued from his cell that one has a moral duty to break unjust laws, openly, lovingly and willing to accept the penalty.
philosophy.practice: Which rule would you be willing to break in public and be punished for?

philosophy.title: Participatory democracy
philosophy.text: Decisions should be made by those who must live with them.
philosophy.practice: What decision affecting you were you never asked about?

philosophy.title: The personal is political
philosophy.text: What looks like a private trouble often has a public cause.
philosophy.practice: Which of your private difficulties do other people share?

philosophy.title: The beloved community
philosophy.text: The end of the struggle is reconciliation, not the defeat of an enemy.
philosophy.practice: Whom would you have to be reconciled with for your cause to be won?

philosophy.title: One-dimensional man
philosophy.text: Herbert Marcuse warned that a comfortable society can absorb every protest and sell it back.
philosophy.practice: What rebellion of yours is really a purchase?

philosophy.title: The medium is the message
philosophy.text: Marshall McLuhan held that the form of a medium shapes us more than anything it carries.
philosophy.practice: What has your phone done to you regardless of what is on it?

philosophy.title: Spaceship Earth
philosophy.text: Seen from the Moon the planet has no borders and no spare parts.
philosophy.practice: What would you do differently if you thought of yourself as crew?

philosophy.title: Access to tools
philosophy.text: Power lies in knowing how to do things for yourself and where to find the means.
philosophy.practice: What tool would change what you are able to do?

intro: The United States entered the 1960s richer than any country had ever been. Wages had doubled since the war, a new suburb went up every week and seventy million children of the baby boom were growing up with television, records and more schooling than any generation before them. By the middle of the decade nearly half the population was under twenty-five. Many of the young looked at the comfortable country they were inheriting and asked why its promises of liberty and equality did not apply to everyone.

The question was first forced by Black Americans in the South. On 1 February 1960 four students sat down at a segregated lunch counter in Greensboro and would not leave. Sit-ins, freedom rides, voter registration drives and marches followed, organised through Black churches and colleges and held to a strict discipline of nonviolence under leaders such as Martin Luther King Jr., Ella Baker, John Lewis and Fannie Lou Hamer. They were met with dogs, fire hoses, bombings and murder, much of it shown on the evening news. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 ended legal segregation and opened the ballot.

The movement taught a generation how to protest. Students who had gone south came back to their campuses and demanded free speech at Berkeley in 1964. As the war in Vietnam grew, with more than half a million American troops there by 1968, teach-ins, draft refusals and marches spread across the country. Women who had been asked to make the coffee at meetings began to meet on their own. The contraceptive pill, approved in 1960, changed the terms of private life. Mexican American farm workers struck in the California vineyards, and in June 1969 patrons of the Stonewall Inn in New York fought back against a police raid.

Alongside the politics ran a revolt in ways of living. In San Francisco and elsewhere the young let their hair grow, moved into shared houses and onto the land, took up Eastern religion, natural food and handmade clothes, and experimented with psychedelic drugs. The music changed with them, and the long-playing album became the art form of the age, from Coltrane and Motown to Dylan, the Beatles and Hendrix. Painters put soup cans in galleries. Engineers working to a deadline set by President Kennedy landed two men on the Moon in July 1969.

The decade was also violent and full of loss. President Kennedy was shot in 1963, Malcolm X in 1965, and King and Robert Kennedy within two months of each other in 1968. Cities burned in Watts, Newark and Detroit. Some fifty-eight thousand Americans and far more Vietnamese died in the war. By the end, parts of the movement had turned to rage, the drug culture had its casualties, and much of the country, which had never joined in, voted for order.

What lasted was large. The legal structure of segregation was gone. The women’s, environmental and gay rights movements that would reshape the following decades had begun. So had an informality in dress and manners, a suspicion of authority and a belief that ordinary people can change public life by acting together.
This Onda takes its practices from that belief: learn the facts, make things yourself, show up in person without violence, speak from experience in a circle and listen all the way through.
guide.origin: The United States, with echoes around the world
guide.era: The decade from 1960 to 1969. Historians often speak of a long sixties, from about 1955 to 1973

figures.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
figures.bio: Baptist minister from Atlanta who led the movement from the Montgomery bus boycott onwards. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 and was murdered in Memphis.

figures.name: Ella Baker
figures.bio: The organiser behind the organisers. She called the students together in 1960 and taught that strong people do not need strong leaders.

figures.name: Fannie Lou Hamer
figures.bio: A Mississippi sharecropper, evicted and beaten for trying to register to vote, who told her story to the Democratic convention of 1964 on live television.

figures.name: John Lewis
figures.bio: A Freedom Rider at twenty-one and chairman of the student committee at twenty-three. His skull was fractured on the bridge at Selma. He later served thirty-three years in Congress.

figures.name: Malcolm X
figures.bio: Minister of the Nation of Islam who preached Black pride and self-defence. After his pilgrimage to Mecca he broke with the Nation and was assassinated in Harlem.

figures.name: Rachel Carson
figures.bio: Marine biologist and writer. She finished Silent Spring while dying of cancer and defended it before Congress.

figures.name: Betty Friedan
figures.bio: Journalist whose book of 1963 reopened the question of women’s lives. She helped found the National Organization for Women in 1966.

figures.name: Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta
figures.bio: Founders of the farm workers’ union. Their grape strike and national boycott, begun in 1965, won contracts for the pickers after five years.

figures.name: Bob Dylan
figures.bio: A singer from Minnesota who arrived in New York in 1961. He gave the folk revival its anthems and then left it behind.

figures.name: Muhammad Ali
figures.bio: Heavyweight champion who refused the draft in 1967 on grounds of conscience and was stripped of his title for three years.

figures.name: Stewart Brand
figures.bio: Biologist and former army officer who campaigned for a photograph of the whole Earth and then published the Whole Earth Catalog.

figures.name: John F. Kennedy
figures.bio: President from 1961. He founded the Peace Corps, set the goal of the Moon and was shot in Dallas on 22 November 1963.

history.detail: Four students of North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College sit at the Woolworth lunch counter. The store desegregates in July.
The Food and Drug Administration approves the first oral contraceptive.
Integrated groups ride buses into the Deep South. One bus is firebombed in Alabama. The government orders terminals desegregated that autumn.
Carson’s book appears in September. In June the students of a small new organisation issue their statement on participatory democracy.
A quarter of a million people gather at the Lincoln Memorial for jobs and freedom. Three months later the president is assassinated.

history.what: Freedom Summer and the Civil Rights Act
history.detail: A thousand volunteers go to Mississippi to register voters and three are murdered. The Act banning segregation is signed on 2 July.
Students at Berkeley surround a police car for thirty-two hours and occupy the administration building. Eight hundred are arrested.

history.what: Selma, the teach-in and the marines
history.detail: Marchers are beaten on the Pettus Bridge on the seventh. The first combat troops land in Vietnam on the eighth. The first teach-in is held on the twenty-fourth.
Federal examiners are sent to register voters. Five days later the Watts district of Los Angeles erupts.
The Black Panther Party is founded in Oakland and the National Organization for Women in Washington.
The Be-In is held in January. Perhaps a hundred thousand young people come to San Francisco. In October fifty thousand march on the Pentagon.
The Tet offensive, the murders of King in April and Robert Kennedy in June, riots in a hundred cities, police violence at the Chicago convention, and Earthrise at Christmas.
Patrons of a gay bar in Greenwich Village resist a police raid, and several nights of protest follow.
Apollo 11 lands on 20 July. In mid-August some four hundred thousand people gather on a farm in New York State for three days of music.

concepts.text: Create a crisis that forces negotiation.
concepts.detail: King listed four steps: collect the facts, negotiate, purify yourself, then act. The action is public, disciplined and accepts the consequences.
An unjust law, King wrote, is one a majority imposes on a minority but does not make binding on itself. To break it and go to jail shows the highest respect for law.

concepts.text: A say in what shapes your life.
concepts.detail: The Port Huron Statement asked that people share in the social decisions that determine the quality and direction of their lives, at work and in school as well as at the ballot box.

concepts.text: Living differently as a form of protest.
concepts.detail: The belief that changing how one eats, dresses, works, loves and worships is itself political, and that a new society can be built in the shell of the old.
Small groups in which each woman spoke in turn about her own life. Patterns that emerged were taken as evidence about society.
A turn from integration toward control of one’s own communities, schools and image. It brought the slogan that Black is beautiful.

concepts.term: The New Frontier and the Great Society
concepts.text: Government as an instrument of hope.
concepts.detail: Kennedy’s and Johnson’s programmes: the Peace Corps, the space programme, Medicare, federal aid to schools and a war on poverty.
Photographs from space and the new science of ecology gave people a picture of the Earth as a single living system with limits.
Through meditation, music, Eastern teaching or psychedelic drugs, many sought experience beyond the everyday self. The drugs harmed a good number of them.

facts.text: The peace symbol was drawn in 1958 by the English designer Gerald Holtom for a march against nuclear weapons. It combines the semaphore signals for N and D.
Three of the four Greensboro students were eighteen and one was seventeen.
King’s best-known passage about his dream was not in his prepared text. The singer Mahalia Jackson called out to him to tell them about the dream.
The Voting Rights Act raised Black voter registration in Mississippi from under seven per cent to nearly sixty in three years.
The Apollo guidance computer had about four kilobytes of working memory.
A message was sent between two computers at universities in California on 29 October 1969. The network became the internet.

Students for a Democratic Society, the largest organisation of the New Left
The system of laws that enforced racial segregation in the Southern states
Compulsory military service, by which most soldiers were sent to Vietnam
The Detroit record company founded by Berry Gordy in 1959, and its sound
Mind-manifesting. A word coined in 1956 for drugs such as LSD, and later for the art and music around them

sensitivity.note: This Onda draws on the methods of the movements of the 1960s. People were beaten, jailed and killed for what is described here, and many who took part are still alive. The practices are offered with respect for them, and are not a costume.
requiredCaveats: Most Americans did not take part in any of this, and the decade also produced a lasting conservative reaction.
The counterculture was largely white and middle class, and it often borrowed carelessly from Native American and Asian traditions.
Drug use damaged and killed many people. Nothing in this Onda asks you to take anything.
Women and gay people were often treated badly inside the movements themselves, which is one reason their own movements began.
